value.overview: The Northern Scrub-Flycatcher (Sublegatus arenarum) is a small, inconspicuous tyrant flycatcher of tropical lowlands. It is associated with dry scrub, open woodland, secondary growth, and mangroves rather than dense mature forest. The species has a scattered distribution from Costa Rica and Panama through northern South America and several Caribbean islands. In Costa Rica, it is a localized Pacific-slope bird and is generally uncommon, making careful attention to habitat and vocalizations useful for finding it.
value.classification: The Northern Scrub-Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers. It is one of several closely related scrub-flycatchers in the genus Sublegatus.
value.identification: This is a small, subdued gray-brown flycatcher with relatively plain plumage. The upperparts are grayish brown, while the throat and underparts are paler, often with a whitish throat and a soft gray wash on the breast and flanks. It has a dark bill, an upright posture, and a fairly long tail. Its restrained appearance can make it difficult to separate from other small flycatchers, so its preferred scrubby habitat, behavior, and distinctive sharp calls are important identification clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The Northern Scrub-Flycatcher has a disjunct range extending from the Pacific lowlands of Costa Rica and Panama through northern Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, and nearby Caribbean islands. It uses open dry scrub, thorny woodland, secondary vegetation, forest edges, and mangroves, generally from sea level to roughly 600 meters. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly on the Pacific slope around the Gulf of Nicoya in the northwest and the Golfo Dulce region in the southwest. It is localized and fairly uncommon in the north, and rarer farther south.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident, not a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals are expected in suitable Pacific lowland habitats throughout the year, especially around the Gulf of Nicoya and Golfo Dulce.
value.breeding: The breeding season is reported mainly from March through June. The nest is a small cup placed in a fork of a tree or shrub, usually only a few meters above the ground. Clutches generally contain two eggs, with incubation lasting about two weeks. Information on fledging and parental care remains limited. In Costa Rica, breeding activity is likely associated with the species' resident Pacific lowland populations, although detailed local nesting information is sparse.
value.dietFeeding: The Northern Scrub-Flycatcher feeds mainly on arthropods, including small insects and other invertebrates, and also takes small fruits. It usually forages low in shrubs and small trees. From an upright perch, it makes short sallies to hover-glean insects or snatch prey and fruit from leaves. Its feeding style is deliberate and localized, matching the dense but open structure of scrub, secondary growth, woodland edges, and mangrove vegetation.
value.behavior: This flycatcher is generally quiet and unobtrusive. It often sits upright on an exposed perch within low vegetation, making short movements to capture food before returning to the same or a nearby perch. Its calls are sharp, brief, and whistled, sometimes given singly or in pairs. Because it is small, plain-colored, and habitat-specific, it can be overlooked even where present. It is most readily detected by combining its calls with observations of low-level foraging behavior.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although detailed population information is limited and regional patterns may differ.
